:::{#def-cuhaz}
#### Cumulative hazard function

The **cumulative hazard function** of a continuous random variable $T$,
often denoted $\cuhaz(t)$ or $\H(t)$,
is the integral of its [hazard function](#def-hazard) up to $t$:

$$\cuhaz(t) \eqdef \int_{u=-\infty}^{t} \haz(u)\,du$$

:::

::: notes

For a non-negative $T$, such as a time to event,
$\haz(u) = 0$ for $u < 0$,
so the lower limit of the integral can be replaced by $0$:
$\cuhaz(t) = \int_{u=0}^{t} \haz(u)\,du$.
That is the form most survival-analysis texts use.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-exp-cumhaz}
#### Cumulative hazard function of an exponential distribution

Continuing @exm-exp-haz,
the hazard is $\haz(u) = \lambda$ for $u \ge 0$ and $0$ for $u < 0$,
so for $t \ge 0$:

$$
\ba
\cuhaz(t)
&= \int_{u=-\infty}^{0} 0\,du + \int_{u=0}^{t} \lambda\,du
&& \text{(split the integral at } 0 \text{)} \\
&= 0 + \lambda t
&& \text{(integrate each piece)} \\
&= \lambda t
&& \text{(simplify)}
\ea
$$

and $\cuhaz(t) = 0$ for $t < 0$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#cor-surv-int-haz}
#### Survival function from the cumulative hazard

If $T$ is a continuous random variable
whose CDF $F$ is differentiable at all but finitely many points,
then for every $t$ with $\surv(t) > 0$:

$$\cuhaz(t) = -\logf{\surv(t)}$$

and therefore:

$$\surv(t) = \expf{-\cuhaz(t)}$$ {#eq-surv-int-haz}

:::

::: proof

Since $\surv(t) = 1 - F(t)$ (@thm-survival-expressions-1)
and $F$ has derivative $f$ wherever $F$ is differentiable (@thm-density-vs-CDF),
$\surv$ has derivative $-f$ at those points.
At each such $u$ with $\surv(u) > 0$:

$$
\ba
\frac{d}{du}\paren{-\logf{\surv(u)}}
&= -\frac{1}{\surv(u)} \cd \frac{d}{du}\surv(u)
&& \text{(chain rule)} \\
&= -\frac{1}{\surv(u)} \cd \paren{-f(u)}
&& \text{(} \surv' = -f \text{)} \\
&= \frac{f(u)}{\surv(u)}
&& \text{(simplify)} \\
&= \haz(u)
&& \text{(hazard equals density over survival)}
\ea
$$

The function $-\logf{\surv(u)}$ is continuous,
because $\surv$ is continuous for a continuous $T$,
and it has derivative $\haz(u)$ at all but finitely many points,
so it is an antiderivative of $\haz$
for the fundamental theorem of calculus.
As $u \to -\infty$, $\surv(u) \to 1$, so $-\logf{\surv(u)} \to 0$.
Therefore:

$$
\ba
\cuhaz(t)
&\eqdef \int_{u=-\infty}^{t} \haz(u)\,du
&& \text{(definition of the cumulative hazard)} \\
&= \sb{-\logf{\surv(u)}}_{u=-\infty}^{t}
&& \text{(} -\log \surv \text{ is an antiderivative of } \haz \text{)} \\
&= -\logf{\surv(t)} - 0
&& \text{(evaluate at the bounds)} \\
&= -\logf{\surv(t)}
&& \text{(simplify)}
\ea
$$

Exponentiating both sides of $-\cuhaz(t) = \logf{\surv(t)}$
gives @eq-surv-int-haz.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-exp-surv-int-haz}
#### Recovering the exponential survival function from its cumulative hazard

Continuing @exm-exp-cumhaz, for $t \ge 0$:

$$
\ba
\surv(t)
&= \expf{-\cuhaz(t)}
&& \text{(survival function from the cumulative hazard)} \\
&= \expf{-\lambda t}
&& \text{(substitute } \cuhaz(t) = \lambda t \text{)}
\ea
$$

which matches the survival function computed directly
in @exm-exp-survfn.

:::
